### Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends entirely on what you’re trying to analyse, how much material you have, and whether you care more about sensitivity, speed, or robustness. Below is a quick‑reference guide summarising the most common techniques used today (in no particular order) along with their typical strengths/weaknesses so you can pick the one that fits your needs. | Ionisation Technique | Typical Applications | Key Strengths | Common Limitations | |----------------------|---------------------|---------------|--------------------| | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Small molecules, peptides/proteins, metabolites, polar organics | • Soft ionisation → preserves noncovalent complexes
• Good quantitative reproducibility
• Works directly from LC eluents | • Requires relatively high solvent flow rates (unless coupled to nanoLC)
• Poor for very hydrophobic/nonpolar compounds unless derivatised | | **Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteomics, polymers, glycans, inorganic salts, large biomolecules (>10 kDa) | • Handles huge masses without fragmentation
• Fast acquisition (single-shot per spot)
• Minimal matrix interference after optimisation | • Sample prep critical – requires uniform crystal formation
• Limited dynamic range compared to ESI | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Semi‑volatile organic compounds, pharmaceuticals, lipids | • Similar workflow to ESI but better for less polar analytes
• Can handle higher concentrations | • Less effective for highly polar species | | **Fast Atom Bombardment / Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (FAIMS/APPI)** | Nonpolar aromatics, explosives, environmental samples | • Very selective ion filtering (reduces chemical noise)
• Useful when background suppression is essential | • More complex instrumentation & tuning required | | **Laser Ablation Electrospray Ionisation (LAESI)** | Direct tissue imaging, solid–solid sampling | • Enables spatially resolved MS without extensive extraction steps | • Lower throughput than conventional LC-MS | | **Desorption Electrospray Ionisation (DESI)** | Ambient surface sampling, forensic evidence | • Near real‑time analysis at ambient pressure | • Surface heterogeneity may affect repeatability | --- #### How to decide: 1. **Sample polarity** * Polar, aqueous solutions → **ESI** (or APCI if slightly less polar). * Hydrophobic solids or powders → **MALDI**, possibly combined with a suitable matrix. 2. **Mass range** * <2000 Da → both ESI and MALDI work well. * >5000 Da (proteins, polymers) → prefer **MALDI** or **nanoESI**. 3. **Quantitation accuracy** * High precision needed → **ESI** (especially with internal standards). 4. **Speed & Throughput** * Rapid screening of many spots → **MALDI** (laser shot per spot). * Continuous liquid chromatography coupling → **ESI**. 5. **Complexity of Matrix** * Complex biological matrices (blood, urine) → **ESI** with strong chromatographic separation first. * Solid surfaces or tissues → consider **DESI** or **LAESI**. 6. **Instrumentation Availability** * If only a single instrument is available, choose the mode that covers the widest mass range while still giving acceptable sensitivity—often this ends up being **ESI** because it works across a broad spectrum of chemistries. --- #### Quick Recommendation Scenarios | Scenario | Suggested Method(s) | Why | |----------|-------------------|-----| | Analyzing intact proteins (~50 kDa) from cell lysates | **NanoESI + Orbitrap** | Ultra‐soft ionisation, excellent resolution | | Profiling small drug metabolites (<300 Da) in plasma | **ESI** (positive/negative modes) | Sensitive, compatible with LC cleanup | | Imaging lipid distribution in brain slices | **MALDI-MSI** | Spatial mapping capability | | Detecting trace explosives on clothing | **APPI** or **FAIMS** | Selective ionisation under ambient conditions | | Quantifying pesticides in soil extracts | **GC‑MS** with **Electron Capture Ionisation (ECI)** | Best for halogenated organics | --- ### Bottom line There isn’t a universal “best” ionisation method—it’s all about matching the physics of the technique to the chemistry of your target and the practical constraints of your experiment. If you let me know: * What class of compound you’re analysing, * Whether you need quantification or just detection, * And any instrumental limits you face, I can narrow down the choice even further!
